content.title: About
content.content: Chicken breast is a lean, boneless cut taken from the bird's chest. When sautéed with a little oil, the skin stays crisp and adds flavor. The dish is high in protein and relatively low in fat when prepared without excess oil.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast is the most consumed chicken cut worldwide because of its low calorie density and high protein content.
When cooked with the skin, the crisp layer retains some B‑vitamins that are naturally present in the skin.
The meat is easily digestible and often recommended in muscle‑building diets.
Different cuisines season it variously—from simple salt and pepper to paprika, garlic, and fresh herbs.
In French cuisine, chicken breast is sometimes sautéed in butter with a splash of white wine for a richer flavor.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 31 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: When cooked properly, the skin absorbs minimal added fat, making the dish suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken breast contains niacin (B3), vitamin B6, and B12, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, important for bones, immune function, and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Satiety support
items.content: The high protein content promotes prolonged fullness, helping with weight management.

items.title: Fat over‑consumption
items.content: Using too much oil or cooking on high heat can cause the skin to soak up excess fat, raising the calorie count.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Chicken must be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C to eliminate salmonella risk.

items.title: Chicken protein allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Adding salt or soy‑based sauces can increase sodium levels, which may be problematic for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sauteed chicken breast with skin can be served as a main course, sliced for salads, added to sandwiches, or tossed with pasta. For a lighter option, trim some of the crisp skin after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked breast to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container. Refrigerate for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in freezer‑safe bags at –18 °C, where it keeps quality for 2‑3 months.
